**On the Color of Shadows**

Here is something that took painters a surprisingly long time to figure out: shadows are not black.

Go outside on a bright day and look at the shadow a tree throws across snow, or across a pale wall, or across a sidewalk. Look at it honestly, without deciding in advance what you're going to see. It is blue. Sometimes violet. Sometimes, near the edges, a faint green where it borrows from the grass. The shadow is not the absence of light; it is a region lit by something other than the sun—by the sky, mostly, which is enormous and blue and pours its color into every place the sun can't reach.

For centuries, European painters rendered shadows as darkened versions of the local color, or as brown, or as a kind of neutral murk. This wasn't stupidity. They were painting what they *knew* rather than what they *saw*, which is what most of us do most of the time. A shadow is where the light isn't; therefore it is dark; therefore paint it dark. The logic is impeccable and the observation is wrong. It took the Impressionists—people willing to stand in a field for hours and be honest about the information arriving at their eyes—to put blue and purple in shadows and get laughed at for it. Monet's haystacks have lavender undersides. Pissarro's snow is streaked with cobalt where the trees block the sun. Critics said it looked like the painters had a disease of the eye. They were seeing correctly for the first time and it looked like madness.

I find this oddly comforting. It suggests that the world is full of things we've all agreed on that are simply not so, and that the correction is always available—you just have to actually look. Not glance, not confirm. Look.

There's a related phenomenon that I like even more. If you sit in a room lit by a single warm bulb, and there's also a window letting in gray daylight, you will see objects casting two shadows: one bluish, cast by the lamp (because the daylight fills it in), and one yellowish, cast by the window (because the lamp fills it in). Each shadow takes the color of the *other* light source. The shadow is never really its own thing. It's a description of everything else that's illuminating the scene. A shadow is a negative space in one light that becomes a positive record of all the remaining light.

You can extend this into a metaphor, and people have, but I'd rather stay with the literal for a while, because the literal is already strange enough.

Consider what your visual system is doing. It receives, on the retina, a patch of dim blue. But your brain does not report "dim blue." It reports "white wall, in shadow." It has performed a calculation: given what I know about the ambient light, what color would this surface have to be to look like this? And it hands you the answer—the surface color—while quietly discarding the actual sensory data. This is called color constancy, and it's wonderful, and it means that you are almost never seeing what's in front of your eyes. You're seeing the brain's best inference about the stuff that light is bouncing off. The painter's trick, the whole discipline of learning to draw, is largely the discipline of overriding that inference and getting back to the raw patch of blue.

Which means, weirdly, that seeing "accurately" and seeing "usefully" are different skills, and they conflict. The brain's version is better for walking through the world. The painter's version is better for making a picture that feels like the world. Both are true. Neither is complete.

I think about this when people argue about whether art is honest. A photograph, we say, is honest. A painting is interpretation. But a camera also has a color-constancy problem—it's called white balance—and the photographer or the sensor is making the same choice the brain makes, deciding what "white" means in this light and adjusting everything else to match. Your phone does this a hundred times a second. It is, in its way, painting. And the Impressionist who puts violet in the snow is, in her way, taking a very unbalanced photograph and refusing to correct it.

Here's something else. The reason the sky is blue is that air scatters short wavelengths more than long ones, so blue light gets bounced around and comes at you from every direction, while red light mostly travels straight from the sun. This is also why sunsets are orange: the light is traveling through so much atmosphere that most of the blue has been scattered away before it reaches you. So the blueness in a shadow is, in a sense, sunlight that took the long way. It left the sun, hit a nitrogen molecule twenty kilometers up, got redirected, hit another, got redirected again, and eventually wandered down into the shade under your tree and lit it faintly from above. The shadow is full of light that got lost on the way here.

I don't want to over-sweeten that. But it does seem worth noticing that the thing we treat as darkness—the shadow, the place the direct light can't reach—is actually the place where all the indirect light gathers and becomes visible. In full sun, the sky's blue is drowned out. In shadow, it finally shows.

I suspect most of what's interesting about the world works this way. The obvious thing is obvious; it announces itself. The subtle thing is there too, underneath, tinting everything, and you only see it when the obvious thing is blocked. You have to get out of the direct light. You have to stand in the shade and wait for your eyes to adjust and then look, without deciding beforehand what color it's supposed to be.

Blue. It's blue. It was always blue. You just had to stop knowing it was black.
